editorial:
Dick Tracy (1937) is a 15-chapter Republic Pictures serial, produced by Nat Levine according to the Internet Archive description. It shares its title and character with the Dick Tracy comic strip. Complete copies circulate on the Internet Archive. A creator might use it for episodic clips, period crime-serial material, or a full-length watch-along.

The rights trap is that this is a 1937 film built on a long-running franchise. For a film from this era, public domain status depends on a missing notice or a missing renewal in the 1964-1965 window. I could not confirm either, so the print stays undetermined. Even if the serial's own copyright lapsed, any underlying strip rights and the Dick Tracy character and name may be separate rights, and I did not verify their status. Check the renewal records and any active trademark before you use the title or character in new work, or on merchandise. A public domain label on an Internet Archive item is the uploader's, and it does not prove the film's status.
faq: Is the 1937 Dick Tracy serial public domain?

Not confirmed. A 1937 film is public domain only if its notice was missing or its renewal was never filed in year 27 or 28 (1964-1965). I did not verify either. Search the Copyright Office public catalog and the Catalog of Copyright Entries for 1964-1965 yourself before relying on it. Copies and labels on the Internet Archive do not prove the film's status.
Can I use the Dick Tracy name or character if the serial print is free?

Not safely. The serial shares its name and character with the Dick Tracy comic strip, which would have its own copyright that I did not check. The name and character may also carry trademark protection, which does not expire with copyright. Even if the print is clear, you would need to clear the character and title for new works or merchandise.
